title: Hardware and AI: a co-evolution
text:
CHAPTER 20. REFLECTIONS
SECTION 20.1. HARDWARE AND AI: A CO-EVOLUTION

This book began with switches: Boole's algebra (Section 1.1), Shannon's relay circuits (Section 2.1), vacuum tubes (Chapter 4) and transistors (Chapter 5). It ends with language models running on chips containing more than a hundred billion transistors. Looking back, the history of artificial intelligence cannot be separated from the history of hardware. Ideas often waited decades for machines able to test them, and machines were reshaped by the ideas that proved most useful. This section reviews that co-evolution, with some numbers to make the scale concrete, and considers where it may go next. For a mechatronics engineer, it is a reminder that algorithms are always physical: every multiplication costs time, area and energy.

1. Ideas waiting for machines

Many central AI ideas were proposed long before hardware could support them:

  - Artificial neurons (McCulloch and Pitts, 1943; Section 7.2) and learning rules (Hebb 1949; Rosenblatt 1958; Widrow-Hoff 1960; Chapter 10) were simulated on computers capable of thousands of operations per second, or built as special analog hardware like the Mark I Perceptron.
  - Backpropagation was described several times between the 1960s and 1980s (Chapter 13), but networks remained small for decades.
  - Convolutional networks worked for digit recognition by 1989-1998 (Section 13.3), and LSTMs were introduced in 1997 (Section 13.4), but neither could be scaled to large images or long texts with the computers of the time.
  - The scale of AlexNet (2012, Section 16.2) required two GPUs with about 3 GB of memory each; the same computation would have been impractical a decade earlier.

The pattern recurs: methods that look weak at one scale of computation become strong at a larger one. Rich Sutton's "bitter lesson" (Section 18.3) makes the same point about general methods that scale with computation.

2. A sense of scale

ENIAC (Section 4.3) could perform 5,000 additions per second per accumulator. Training GPT-3 (Section 18.3) took about 3.15 x 10^23 floating-point operations. At 5,000 operations per second, that would take about 6.3 x 10^19 seconds, roughly 2 trillion years, around 150 times the age of the universe. On 1,000 modern data-center GPUs sustaining, say, 400 trillion operations per second each (a plausible figure for 16-bit arithmetic on 2020s accelerators, though actual utilization varies), it would take about 7.9 x 10^5 seconds, about 9 days.

The growth of training compute has been measured. OpenAI's "AI and Compute" analysis (Dario Amodei and Danny Hernandez, 2018) estimated that compute for the largest training runs had doubled about every 3.4 months between 2012 and 2018. Jaime Sevilla and colleagues ("Compute Trends Across Three Eras of Machine Learning," 2022) found that before 2010 training compute grew in line with Moore's law, doubling roughly every 20 months, and since the early 2010s about every 6 months, with a separate "large-scale" trend of even bigger models from late 2015. These rates are far faster than Moore's law (Section 6.2); the difference came from spending more money, using more chips in parallel, and from more efficient chips and number formats.

3. Why GPUs, and why matrix multiplication

The success of deep learning depended on an accident of hardware history. GPUs were designed for graphics (Section 15.1), which requires applying the same operations to millions of pixels and vertices in parallel. Neural networks, it turned out, are dominated by the same kind of work: dense matrix multiplication. A layer computing y = W x for a batch of inputs is a matrix-matrix product, with high arithmetic intensity (many operations per byte loaded, Section 15.1's roofline model). Convolutions and attention (Sections 13.3 and 18.1) can be written as matrix multiplications too.

Researchers then shaped their models to fit the hardware. The transformer won partly because it replaced the sequential recurrence of RNNs with parallel matrix products (Section 18.1). Sara Hooker's essay "The Hardware Lottery" (2020) argued that research ideas often succeed or fail because of how well they suit available hardware and software, not only because of their intrinsic merit. Ideas such as capsule networks or sparse, event-driven networks may have been disadvantaged because they do not map well onto GPUs.

4. Hardware shaped for AI

As AI became the main use of large-scale computing, hardware adapted to it:

  - Reduced precision. Neural networks tolerate low-precision arithmetic. Training moved from 32-bit floating point to 16-bit formats (FP16 with loss scaling, as described in "Mixed Precision Training," Paulius Micikevicius and colleagues, 2017; and bfloat16, which keeps FP32's 8-bit exponent with a shorter mantissa), and inference to 8-bit integers and later to 8-bit, 4-bit and even smaller floating-point formats. Halving the number of bits roughly halves memory and bandwidth needs and allows more arithmetic units per chip area.
  - Tensor cores. NVIDIA's Volta architecture (V100, 2017) introduced tensor cores, units that multiply small matrices (4 x 4 in FP16, accumulating in higher precision) in one operation. Each later generation (Ampere, Hopper, Blackwell) increased their throughput and added lower-precision formats. NVIDIA's H100 (Hopper, 2022) has 80 billion transistors; the Blackwell B200 package (2024) combines two dies totaling 208 billion.
  - Google's TPU. Google deployed its first Tensor Processing Unit in its data centers in 2015 and described it in 2017 (Norman Jouppi and colleagues, "In-Datacenter Performance Analysis of a Tensor Processing Unit"). Its core is a systolic array of 65,536 8-bit multiply-accumulate units (256 x 256), peaking at 92 trillion operations per second, with 28 MiB of on-chip memory. In a systolic array, data flows rhythmically between neighboring units, each doing a multiply-accumulate and passing values on, so each operand fetched from memory is reused many times. Google reported it was on average about 15 to 30 times faster on its inference workloads than a contemporary GPU or CPU. Later TPU generations supported training and were connected into "pods" of thousands of chips; GPT-scale models such as PaLM and Gemini were trained on them.
  - Other accelerators: Cerebras built "wafer-scale" chips occupying an entire silicon wafer; Groq, Graphcore, AWS (Trainium, Inferentia), Huawei (Ascend) and many startups designed AI chips; and phones gained neural processing units for on-device inference.

5. The memory wall

Arithmetic has become cheap compared with moving data. Mark Horowitz's widely cited estimates for a 45-nanometer process (ISSCC 2014) put a 32-bit floating-point multiply at about 3.7 picojoules, but a 32-bit read from off-chip DRAM at about 640 picojoules, more than 170 times as much. Modern processes change the numbers but not the pattern. This is why:

  - AI accelerators use high-bandwidth memory (HBM): stacks of DRAM dies placed next to the processor in the same package, connected with thousands of wires, giving several terabytes per second of bandwidth.
  - Algorithms are designed to reuse data on chip: tiled matrix multiplication (Section 15.2), FlashAttention, operator fusion, and the KV cache (Section 18.1).
  - Generating text one token at a time is usually limited by memory bandwidth, not arithmetic: every generated token requires reading all the model's weights from memory. For a model with 70 billion parameters stored in 16 bits (140 GB), at 3 TB/s, each token would take at least about 47 milliseconds if run on one device with the weights read once per step, which is why batching many users' requests together, quantizing weights and spreading models across chips matter so much.

At the scale of whole systems, the network between chips is also critical: training a frontier model requires tens of thousands of accelerators working in parallel with data, tensor and pipeline parallelism (Section 15.2), linked by very fast interconnects, and the limit is often communication rather than computation.

6. Energy and physical limits

Dennard scaling ended in the mid-2000s (Section 6.2): transistors kept shrinking, but power per transistor stopped falling proportionally, so chips became limited by heat. Performance gains since then have come from parallelism and specialization rather than faster clocks. For AI, the result is enormous total power use. Data centers for AI training and inference in the mid-2020s were planned at hundreds of megawatts to gigawatts each, comparable to the output of large power plants, and their electricity needs became a factor in energy planning in several countries (Section 20.2).

Physics still offers room for efficiency. The brain runs on roughly 20 watts, a figure often quoted, though comparing it with digital hardware is difficult because the brain computes very differently. Research directions include:

  - Neuromorphic chips, such as IBM's TrueNorth (2014) and Intel's Loihi (2017-2018), which use spiking neurons and event-driven communication, inspired by the neuron models of Chapter 7.
  - Analog and in-memory computing, which performs multiply-accumulate operations inside memory arrays using physical laws (Ohm's law for multiplication, Kirchhoff's current law for addition), avoiding data movement, at the cost of noise and limited precision; this returns, in a sense, to the analog computing of the mid-twentieth century.
  - Optical computing, using light for matrix operations and for communication between chips.
  - Advanced packaging (chiplets, 3D stacking) and new transistor structures (gate-all-around), continuing Moore's law in modified form.

7. Hardware as geopolitics

By the 2020s, the hardware for AI depended on a remarkably concentrated supply chain: chip designs from a few companies, above all NVIDIA; manufacturing of the most advanced chips mainly by TSMC in Taiwan; extreme ultraviolet lithography machines from one company, ASML in the Netherlands; and high-bandwidth memory from a few Korean and American firms. In October 2022, the United States introduced export controls restricting sales of advanced AI chips and chipmaking equipment to China, later tightened several times; China invested heavily in domestic alternatives. Access to computing power became a matter of national strategy, as access to oil had been in the twentieth century. The co-evolution of hardware and AI is now also a co-evolution of technology and politics.

8. Lessons from the long view

  - Switching elements changed (relays, tubes, transistors, and integrated circuits), but the logical foundations (Boolean algebra, Turing's universal machine, the stored-program design) remained.
  - Each jump in hardware capability opened new possibilities for AI: symbolic AI on early mainframes, expert systems on minicomputers and workstations, statistical learning on clusters, and deep learning on GPUs and TPUs.
  - Successful AI methods are those that turn more computation into better results, and successful hardware is shaped by the computations that matter most. Each drives the other.
  - The constraints that matter today are energy, memory bandwidth, communication and supply chains, rather than the number of transistors alone. Engineers who understand both the algorithms and the physics will design the next generation.

9. Summary

  - Many AI ideas (neurons, backpropagation, CNNs, LSTMs) waited decades for enough computation.
  - Training compute for large models doubled about every 6 months from the early 2010s (Sevilla and colleagues), far faster than Moore's law; GPT-3's 3 x 10^23 operations would have taken ENIAC trillions of years.
  - Deep learning's reliance on dense matrix multiplication made GPUs, and then tensor cores and TPUs (systolic arrays, deployed 2015), its natural hardware; "the hardware lottery" shaped which ideas succeeded.
  - Data movement costs far more energy than arithmetic, driving HBM, on-chip reuse, low precision and memory-bandwidth-aware algorithms.
  - Energy, physical limits and a concentrated global supply chain have made AI hardware a central technical, economic and political issue.
